entries.1:1: Paul writes this letter while he is in prison for his faith, and he includes Timothy with him. He is writing to Philemon, a man he loves and who has been a real help to other believers.
entries.1:2: Paul also greets Apphia, Archippus, and the whole group of believers who meet in Philemon's home. This shows the letter is personal but also meant to be heard by the church.
entries.1:3: Paul wishes them God's kindness and peace, coming from the Father and from Jesus. These are not just polite words but a prayer that they would truly experience God's goodness.
entries.1:4: Paul regularly thanks God for Philemon and prays for him. It shows how much Paul values him and cares about his spiritual life.
entries.1:5: Paul has heard about Philemon's love and faith, both toward Jesus and toward all God's people. His faith is not just a belief but shows itself in how he treats others.
entries.1:6: Paul prays that the faith Philemon shares with others would become effective and fruitful. He wants him to deeply understand and live out every good thing God has given him for Christ's sake.
entries.1:7: Philemon's love has brought Paul great joy and encouragement, because he has refreshed and strengthened other believers. His kindness has made a real difference in people's lives.
entries.1:8: Paul says he has the right, as an apostle, to simply command Philemon to do the right thing. But he chooses not to use that authority here.
entries.1:9: Instead, out of love, Paul appeals to Philemon as a personal request. He reminds him that he is an old man and now a prisoner for Christ's sake.
entries.1:10: Paul is asking a favor for Onesimus, whom he led to faith while in prison. He calls him his child because of that spiritual relationship.
entries.1:11: Onesimus used to be useless to Philemon, but now he has become genuinely useful to both Paul and Philemon. His life has changed.
entries.1:12: Paul is sending Onesimus back to Philemon, even though he is very dear to Paul. He is giving up someone he loves for Philemon's sake.
entries.1:13: Paul would have liked to keep Onesimus with him to help him while he is in prison for the gospel. He would have been serving Paul on Philemon's behalf.
entries.1:14: But Paul refuses to do anything without Philemon's consent. He wants Philemon's kindness to be a free choice, not something forced on him.
entries.1:15: Paul suggests that maybe Onesimus was separated from Philemon for a while so that he could come back to him permanently. God can use even hard situations for good.
entries.1:16: Onesimus is no longer just a servant but a beloved brother in Christ. He is especially dear to Paul, and even more so to Philemon, both as a person and as a fellow believer.
entries.1:17: Paul asks Philemon to welcome Onesimus just as he would welcome Paul himself. If Philemon considers Paul a partner and friend, he should receive Onesimus the same way.
entries.1:18: If Onesimus has wronged Philemon or owes him anything, Paul says to charge it to him. He is willing to take on the debt himself.
entries.1:19: Paul writes this promise in his own handwriting: he will pay it back. He gently reminds Philemon that he owes Paul his very life, meaning his spiritual life through Paul's ministry.
entries.1:20: Paul asks Philemon to do this for him as a brother, so that he can have joy and be refreshed in Christ. He is appealing to their friendship and shared faith.
entries.1:21: Paul is confident that Philemon will do what he asks, and even more. He trusts his character and generosity.
entries.1:22: Paul asks Philemon to prepare a room for him, because he hopes to be released and visit them through their prayers. This shows Paul expected to see him again.
entries.1:23: Epaphras, who is in prison with Paul for Christ's sake, sends his greetings. He is a fellow believer and companion in suffering.
entries.1:24: Mark, Aristarchus, Demas, and Luke also send their greetings. They are Paul's fellow workers in spreading the gospel.
entries.1:25: Paul closes by asking that the grace of the Lord Jesus Christ be with their spirit. It is a final blessing and prayer for God's kindness to remain with them.
